title: How Good Journalism Fights Bad Science
paragraphs: Every day, news outlets report on new scientific discoveries, often with exciting headlines claiming that a certain food prevents cancer or that a new treatment could transform medicine. Unfortunately, such claims are frequently exaggerated. Research suggests that the problem often begins before journalists even become involved, and that careful, critical journalism plays an essential role in protecting the public from misleading science.

One influential study, published in the British Medical Journal in 2014, examined 462 press releases issued by 20 leading universities in the UK, along with 668 news stories based on them. Press releases are short documents that universities and research institutions send to journalists to promote new studies. The researchers found that about 40% of the press releases contained exaggerations. For example, some overstated the strength of the evidence, suggesting that one factor caused another when the study only showed a link between them. Others implied that results from experiments on animals applied directly to humans, or gave readers advice that the research did not support.

Crucially, when press releases contained such exaggerations, news stories were much more likely to repeat them. However, when press releases were accurate, the rate of exaggeration in news stories was far lower. Surprisingly, exaggerated press releases did not lead to more news coverage, which suggests that accuracy does not necessarily come at the cost of attention. The authors concluded that academics and their institutions must take responsibility for their own press releases.

Nevertheless, journalists also share responsibility. A later study from South Africa compared university press releases with the media articles based on them, and found that a third of the articles overstated the research findings. In many cases, the exaggeration had been added by the publication, rather than coming from the press release. Critics refer to the practice of copying press releases with little independent checking as "churnalism."

So what does good science journalism look like? Experts argue that, at a minimum, journalists should read the original study and check whether its results actually match the claims in the press release. Ideally, they should also interview independent experts who were not involved in the research and can place the findings in context. Good reporting also explains a study's limitations, such as a small sample size, or the difference between correlation and causation.
By asking critical questions, responsible journalists can help prevent misleading claims from spreading.
